{"id": "74:34/q12", "question": "What ancillary material appears in the added source passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "74:34/q12/p1", "position": "Al-Damghani also lists senses of saqat: regret, falling into shirk, scattering, and literal falling.", "reasons": "Al-Damghani gives this separate lexical entry alongside the extracted dawn gloss."}, {"id": "74:34/q12/p2", "position": "Al-Suyuti explains the abridgment, title, and prayer attached to his report collection.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti says he condensed his multivolume isnad-based Tafsir Musnad to provide hadith texts without long chains while retaining text and reliable-book references. He titles it al-Durr al-manthur fi al-tafsir bi-l-ma'thur and asks God to guard its author against error and falsehood."}, {"id": "74:34/q12/p3", "position": "The collection gives reports about al-Fatihah's Qur'anic status, codex inclusion, and Meccan revelation.", "reasons": "Ibrahim reports al-Aswad's affirmation that al-Fatihah is Qur'an, transmitted by Abd ibn Humayd. Reports from Muhammad ibn Sirin and Ibn al-Anbari say Ubayy wrote al-Fatihah, the two protective suras, and invocations whereas Ibn Masud wrote none. Uthman wrote al-Fatihah and the protective suras; Ibn Masud said he would have placed al-Fatihah at the beginning of everything had he written it. Ali says it came down in Mecca from a treasure beneath the Throne, transmitted by al-Wahidi and al-Tha'labi."}, {"id": "74:34/q12/p4", "position": "Abu Maysarah reports the Prophet's account to Khadijah of hearing a voice while alone.", "reasons": "Abu Maysarah Amr ibn Shurahbil says the Prophet feared what the voice meant and Khadijah answered, 'God forbid.'"}, {"id": "74:34/q12/p5", "position": "The Itqan reports derivations and differing definitions of tafsir and ta'wil.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti reports ta'wil derived from return or governance. Abu Ubayd and others identify tafsir with ta'wil; Ibn Habib objects to treating them as synonyms. Al-Raghib calls tafsir broader and word-focused, ta'wil meaning- and sentence-focused. Other accounts distinguish a word with one sense from choosing among several by evidence, or categorical divine intent from ranked possibilities (al-Maturidi), or lexical evidence from inward intended reality (Abu Talib al-Taghlibi, with his watchful-ambush example)."}, {"id": "74:34/q12/p6", "position": "The Majaz passage illustrates emphasis through repetition in other Qur'anic wording.", "reasons": "The author of Majaz says repetition emphasizes a point, citing repeated 'I saw' and 'awla laka,' the restatement of three plus seven as ten, and repeated curses on Abu Lahab."}, {"id": "74:34/q12/p7", "position": "Qatadah identifies one of the great calamities as the Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti reports Qatadah's identification of one of the great calamities as the Fire alongside his dawn gloss."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q01", "question": "Why does the verse say 'Indeed We created'?", "turns_on": "Which divine act and audience require emphasis?", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q01/p1", "position": "The emphatic divine subject answers the opening question and stresses God's sole creation against denial.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says idolaters act as deniers by worshipping what did not create. Sāmarrāʾī says the opening question elicits assent; initial creation, reproduction, testing and judgment require emphasis, unlike ordinary parental generation (45:24; 34:7). The same divine subject creates, tests and equips people."}, {"id": "76:2/q01/p2", "position": "The emphatic attribution of guidance echoes this creation formula.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says guidance, enabling worship (51:56), may deserve even greater emphasis; the revelation statement adds three emphasis markers because Quraysh disputed revelation more than creation (31:25; 39:38)."}, {"id": "76:2/q01/p3", "position": "The contrast with 'We created them' later reflects the opening's contested creation and testing.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī raises the wording contrast, then explains that the opening includes initial creation and a disputed purpose; ordinary reproduction is accepted."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q02", "question": "Who is 'the human' created from a mixed drop?", "turns_on": "Whether the generic noun can include Adam when creation here is from a drop.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q02/p1", "position": "Adam's descendants, or humankind generically as reproduced from a drop.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī calls this the commentators' consensus; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and Ṭabāṭabāʾī reason that Adam was not made from semen. Al-Biqāʿī takes a generic term narrowed here to descendants. Bursawī prefers species in both verses, invoking resurrection."}, {"id": "76:2/q02/p2", "position": "Adam is included, either with all humans or through a nonhuman drop of origin.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī generalizes the noun to Adam and descendants. Elmalılı says clay verses (3:59; 23:12; 30:20; 35:11; 40:67; 6:2; 55:14) do not exclude a nonhuman nuṭfa for Adam. Al-Nasafī and Study Quran report Adam or both as options."}, {"id": "76:2/q02/p3", "position": "The first verse may mean Adam, while this verse means his descendants.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports and declines this reading; Sāmarrāʾī says it displays continued generation and divine power. Al-Nasafī reports an Adam reading linked to his time before recognition."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q03", "question": "Why is 'the human' repeated instead of a pronoun?", "turns_on": "Whether definite repetition identifies the same referent or highlights a changed one.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q03/p1", "position": "The explicit noun magnifies creation and emphasizes humanity as its subject.", "reasons": "Bursawī says it reinforces the statement; Ālūsī says it stresses the material; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it records God's creation and governance; Suyūṭī identifies explicit repetition as magnification. Burhān connects repetition with restoration of creation and human creation's greatness."}, {"id": "76:2/q03/p2", "position": "Repetition can mark different referents, Adam first and descendants second.", "reasons": "Bahāʾ al-Dīn cites this and other definite noun examples against a rigid identity rule; Burhān adduces scriptural and sovereignty counterexamples. Suyūṭī says some apparent counterexamples use generic definites and do not overturn the rule."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q04", "question": "What does nuṭfah denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the word names the man's emission or the joined generative material.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q04/p1", "position": "A small quantity of liquid, especially reproductive fluid.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, al-Jishumī, Qurṭubī and others trace it to liquid in a vessel; Ibn Rawāḥa's waterskin verse illustrates it, and Thaʿlabī relates its root to dripping. Ṭabrisī notes that it can also mean a river, citing ʿAlī on Nahrawān, and poetry illustrates a drop in a basin. Raghib calls it pure water; Elmalılı cites 75:37 and a Muslim report that generation is from part of semen."}, {"id": "76:2/q04/p2", "position": "Here it is the man's semen, later mingled with the woman's contribution.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this alternative to calling the joined fluids the drop; Jishumī calls its primary referent male fluid. Asad supplies the unstated female ovum (86:6–7)."}, {"id": "76:2/q04/p3", "position": "Here it is the already combined male and female reproductive fluids.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives al-Suddī's view; Thaʿlabī calls both fluids nuṭfah. Elmalılı questions this timing: after fusion the product is an embryo or clot."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q05", "question": "What does amshāj mean in Arabic usage?", "turns_on": "Whether the gloss describes general mixing or specifically varied color.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q05/p1", "position": "Mixed or mixtures; mashj, mashaj and mashīj are cited as related forms.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Farrāʾ, lexicographers and commentators define the root as mixing. Ruʾbah's mixed blood, Abū Dhuʾayb's mixed adjective, al-Shammākh's mixture, and a Hudhalī arrow furnish poetic evidence; Ibn al-Aʿrābī supplies variant singular forms. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes variant witnesses to an interlaced-image line."}, {"id": "76:2/q05/p2", "position": "Its root can also describe a mixture of two colors.", "reasons": "Yamān and Ibn al-Aʿrābī supply this usage; Suyūṭī glosses the word as mixed in color."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q06", "question": "What are the mixtures in the drop?", "turns_on": "The identity of what is mingled and whether amshāj describes one drop or later stages.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q06/p1", "position": "The male and female reproductive fluids mingle.", "reasons": "Ikrima, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and al-Rabīʿ recur across sources; Ṭabarī and Rāzī prefer it because a clot is no longer a nuṭfah. Rāzī links 86:7; Mujāhid links 49:13; Asad specifies ovum. Al-Biqāʿī and Bayḍāwī stress different properties and organ contributions. Elmalılı objects that fusion is too late for the term nuṭfah."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p2", "position": "Different colors within or between the fluids are the mixtures.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ḍaḥḥāk and others report red, white, yellow, green or black combinations; specific assignments differ. Many language scholars prefer the color account. Ālūsī reports a green tint after remaining in the womb. Ṭabarī objects that male fluid is known as one color."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p3", "position": "The word covers successive embryonic stages from drop to clot, morsel, bone and flesh.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima and Qatāda detail stages, sometimes starting with earth, ending in hair or a new creation (23:14). Ṭabarī objects that a clot cannot still be called a drop. Elmalılı extends the sequence before conception; Bursawī gives forty, eighty and 120 day milestones."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p4", "position": "The mixtures are veins or formative lines within the fluid.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd, Usāma's father and Zayd b. Aslam are cited. Aṭāʾ through

Ibn Jurayj compares them to thin sinews; Elmalılı interprets 'roots' as inherited formative traits. Ṭabarī suspects this view may aim at varying colors."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p5", "position": "Semen mixes with blood, including menstrual blood in one account.", "reasons": "Qatāda and al-Zajjāj describe water or semen with blood before clot and morsel; al-Ḥasan says menstruation stops in pregnancy and its blood mingles with the drop. Farrāʾ includes blood and clot; al-Mubarrad specifies semen and blood."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p6", "position": "The constituents are bodily humors or temperaments.", "reasons": "Language scholars list heat, cold, dryness and moisture; another list is blood, phlegm and yellow and black bile, with Elmalılı also naming lymph. Ibn al-Sikkīt ties blending to varied human dispositions."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p7", "position": "The mixture includes different powers or elemental and vital constituents.", "reasons": "Rāghib links powers in the drop to 23:12–14; Rāzī allows earthly elements and air; Ibn ʿĀshūr proposes chemical, vegetal, earthy and vital components."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p8", "position": "It is a stringlike substance emitted after urination from which a child develops.", "reasons": "Two Ibn ʿAbbās reports give this distinctive account."}, {"id": "76:2/q06/p9", "position": "Some soil from each newborn's future burial place is mingled into the drop.", "reasons": "Bursawī transmits this report from the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q07", "question": "How can amshāj describe singular nuṭfah?", "turns_on": "Whether afʿāl can itself be singular, or plural agreement reflects the parts of a single drop.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q07/p1", "position": "Amshāj is plural in form; the single drop contains many mixed components, or an omitted 'possessing mixtures' is understood.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Ibn Qutayba and many grammarians give singulars mashj or mashīj; Wāḥidī likens a composite pot, garment and land. Abū Ḥayyān cites Sibawayh that afʿāl is not singular. Sāmin explains each component can count as a drop. Wāḥidī and Rāzī supply an omitted construct; Arabic examples of generic singular with plural adjective include 55:76."}, {"id": "76:2/q07/p2", "position": "Amshāj is a lexical singular or singular adjective with a plural-looking form.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī compares barmah aʿshār and burd akyās; Nasafī follows. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers this, saying Sibawayh did not explicitly disallow it. Sāmin defends Zamakhsharī as describing agreement through parts; Abū Ḥayyān and the shaykh object that afʿāl is not a singular pattern."}, {"id": "76:2/q07/p3", "position": "Both singular and plural analyses can operate, with different images of mixture.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says singular emphasizes one composite, plural multiple composite elements; Sāmarrāʾī compares other Arabic nouns that can function in either number."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q08", "question": "Why use the plural-looking amshāj?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q08/p1", "position": "Its form stresses the many blended elements within the single drop.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī compares pluralized descriptors for extensive distribution, such as sabāsib and qifār; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the description intensifying; Elmalılı distinguishes a single blend from blends within blends."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q09", "question": "What determines the child's resemblance and bodily contributions?", "turns_on": "Whether precedence or predominance explains resemblance, and how each report assigns material and colors.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q09/p1", "position": "Whichever parent's fluid precedes or prevails determines resemblance; their contributions to the body differ.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAbbās and others assign bone, nerves, strength or nails to the man, flesh, blood, hair or fat to the woman; ʿIkrima also says skin from the man. The fluids are described as thick white and thin yellow. Mujāhid says paternal or maternal uncles are resembled; a Prophetic report through Anas says precedence or dominance decides. A report through Abū Ayyūb asks about the child's sex."}, {"id": "76:2/q09/p2", "position": "The accounts give differing color assignments for each parent's fluid.", "reasons": "Mujāhid variously describes male white/red and female green/red or green/yellow; another report has male white and female green/yellow. These details vary across transmitters."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q10", "question": "What is meant by 'We test him'?", "turns_on": "Whether the trial is prenatal transformation or later accountable life, and which forms of trial are meant.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q10/p1", "position": "God tests the person through later moral duties, commands, prohibitions, and deeds.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī links sound nature and intellect to worship (51:56); Ṭabrisī says duties expose obedience for recompense. Ibn Kathīr cites 67:2; Elmalılı adds hardship, reward, punishment and 75:40. Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī treat later accountability as intended; Ibn ʿĀshūr places it after rational maturity. Al-Biqāʿī says this establishes proof though God already knows."}, {"id": "76:2/q10/p2", "position": "God tests people with good and evil, calling for gratitude in ease and patience in hardship.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and al-Ḥasan identify the test's contrasting circumstances; Ibn ʿAbbās joins transformation through stages to testing by good and evil."}, {"id": "76:2/q10/p3", "position": "Testing names the embryo's passage through successive states.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Zamakhsharī take transfer in the womb as a figurative trial; Bayḍāwī and Sāmin repeat it. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this because hearing and sight follow the test in the text, whereas they enable legal duty."}, {"id": "76:2/q10/p4", "position": "Testing means bringing the human into existence and worldly life.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān attach this sense to creation as a simultaneous circumstance."}, {"id": "76:2/q10/p5", "position": "The verb can mean assigning responsibility or choosing, as well as testing.", "reasons": "Māwardī offers taklīf and religious commands; Jishumī says ibtilāʾ can mean choosing and explains God's action by analogy with a tester so known conduct becomes manifest."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q11", "question": "How does God's testing relate to His prior knowledge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q11/p1", "position": "Testing manifests what God already knows and establishes the basis for accountability.", "reasons": "Jishumī says God acts as a tester without acquiring knowledge; Ṭabrisī says obedience and disobedience become evident for recompense. Biqāʿī says the test establishes proof in human terms; Bursawī distinguishes general foreknowledge from manifested acceptance and rejection."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q12", "question": "How does nَbtalīhi connect grammatically to the surrounding clauses?", "turns_on": "Whether testing temporally follows the senses, is intended at creation, or describes creation itself.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q12/p1", "position": "It is a prospective circumstantial clause: God created the human intending a later test.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Nasafī and others connect it to creation; Sāmin says it can qualify creator or human, and legal accountability makes it prospective. Sāmarrāʾī cites 37:112, 48:27 and 90:4 for future states; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it is advanced for emphasis, while guidance follows in 76:3."}, {"id": "76:2/q12/p2", "position": "It is a purpose clause with an omitted lām: creation is so that God may test.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares ordinary expressions and 74:6; Sāmarrāʾī compares 67:2 and says the unprefixed form admits both purpose and circumstance."}, {"id": "76:2/q12/p3", "position": "The clauses are understood in reverse temporal order: God made him hearing and seeing in order to test him.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba reason that senses or completed creation precede testing; Naḥḥās argues the faʾ instead orders events and no purposive lām occurs. Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, Sāmin and Ālūsī call inversion forced or unnecessary; Ṭabāṭabāʾī also rejects using it to rescue a duty reading."}, {"id": "76:2/q12/p4", "position": "The ordinary order stands: creation is for testing, then hearing and sight equip the person.", "reasons": "The composer cited by Wāḥidī attaches test to initial creation, with senses supplied afterward; Ṭabarī says trial needs sound nature and intact mind even without hearing or sight. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reads two coordinated complete clauses; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the result order favors a prenatal trial."}, {"id": "76:2/q12/p5", "position": "It may begin a new sentence: 'We will test him.'", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this alternative."}, {"id": "76:2/q12/p6", "position": "With embryonic transformation, the circumstantial clause is simultaneous with creation.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Sāmin contrast this with the prospective legal-duty reading."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q13", "question": "Why use the form nabtalīhi rather than a lighter verb for testing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q13/p1", "position": "The iftaʿala form intensifies the test and suits this sura's fuller account.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī compares ṣabara/iṣṭabara and kasaba/iktasaba, with 3:154 and 33:11; he cautions that more letters do not always intensify, citing ḥadhar versus ḥādhir. He contrasts al-Mulk's yablūkum (67:2): its forgiving close and briefer treatment of test, unlike this sura's senses, guidance, deeds and outcomes, suit the lighter form."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q14", "question": "What does 'so We made him hearing and seeing' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the words describe bodily faculties alone or the understanding and response they make possible.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q14/p1", "position": "God endowed the human with the physical faculties of hearing and sight.", "reasons": "Qushayrī and Nasafī state the grant; Damghānī cites auditory usage at 3:193 and visual usage at 12:93 and 50:22. Ibn al-Jawzī

defines hearing as perception of sounds and baṣīr as opposite of blind. Muqātil locates the gift after lifeless fetal stages."}, {"id": "76:2/q14/p2", "position": "Hearing and sight also imply intellect, understanding and discernment.", "reasons": "Māwardī contrasts animals; Rāzī reports understanding, obedience and knowledge as interpretations and cites 19:42. Abū Ḥayyān calls the faculties the noblest means of apprehension; Ibn ʿĀshūr says humans perceive and discriminate more than animals. Elmalılı says a human must truly perceive duties."}, {"id": "76:2/q14/p3", "position": "The phrase can mean being able to hear and see guidance.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī records this more specific interpretation."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q15", "question": "What further Arabic senses of hearing and seeing are noted?", "turns_on": "The distinction between direct sensory meaning and other attested root usages.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q15/p1", "position": "The normal senses are perceiving sounds and seeing with the eyes.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī distinguishes samāʿ as perception from samʿ as faculty; baṣīr is opposite blind, and baṣura/abṣara can mean seeing."}, {"id": "76:2/q15/p2", "position": "The roots have extended senses of knowledge, proof and other homonyms.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says baṣar/baṣīr can denote knowledge; baṣīra can mean a blood drop, shield or proof; a poem uses baṣīr for dog. With different vocalization samʿ can mean good renown or a wolf-hyena offspring, and samāʿ can be an imperative 'listen.'"}]}
{"id": "76:2/q16", "question": "How do hearing and sight serve the human test?", "turns_on": "Whether senses are necessary instruments of accountability or themselves the tested gift.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q16/p1", "position": "They equip humans to receive revelation, perceive created signs, judge, and obey or disobey.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī associates auditory revelation and visible signs with the faʾ. Biqāʿī details outward and inward senses, avoiding harm and seeking benefit; Ibn ʿĀshūr assigns hearing to law and sight to proofs. Bursawī says intellect is implicit as their instrument. Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran note both obedience and disobedience are possible (7:179; 7:198; 10:43)."}, {"id": "76:2/q16/p2", "position": "The senses themselves are the means or part of the test.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba's reordered reading tests through the senses; Wāḥidī reports grammarians who understand testing by making one hear and see. Ṭabarī objects that trial remains possible without either faculty, because sound nature and mind are decisive; the senses call for gratitude."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q17", "question": "Why is hearing mentioned before sight?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q17/p1", "position": "Hearing is especially important for receiving address, law and revelation.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says audible signs are clearer; Sāmarrāʾī says a blind person can receive a message more easily than a deaf person. A reported proof notes no prophet was deaf while Jacob became blind; Sāmarrāʾī limits superiority to receiving revelation, not every respect."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q18", "question": "Why use these adjectival forms and join them without a conjunction?", "turns_on": "How the adjective pattern and coordination convey the gift.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q18/p1", "position": "The intensive forms mark the fullness of the favor and human powers.", "reasons": "Bursawī identifies 'seeing' as the second object of 'made'; Ibn ʿĀshūr associates the forms with heightened human discrimination."}, {"id": "76:2/q18/p2", "position": "Samīʿ is suited to praise, while sammāʿ would evoke blame.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī raises the choice and says Qurʾānic samīʿ praises God or people, whereas sammāʿ describes blameworthy listeners (5:41–42; 9:47)."}, {"id": "76:2/q18/p3", "position": "Omitting 'and' makes both faculties attributes of the same human.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says a conjunction might suggest separate groups, one hearing and another seeing."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q19", "question": "What does the sequence of creation, trial and senses teach about humanity?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q19/p1", "position": "Humble origin and intricate formation display God's power, wisdom and human dependence.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr stresses prior insignificance; Biqāʿī describes bones, joints, organs, digestion, circulation and three darknesses to argue for the unseen Maker, contrasting people's admiration of wall designs. Elmalılı rejects autonomous nature and stresses staged cultivation and eventual return; Study Quran emphasizes lowly origin (86:6–7)."}, {"id": "76:2/q19/p2", "position": "Creation aims at accountable worship, and duties distinguish humanity.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī cites 51:56; Elmalılı invokes 67:2 and 75:40. Ibn ʿĀshūr says religious law underlies civilization and leads into guidance; Sāmarrāʾī lists the complete sequence of agents, faculties, choices and outcomes."}, {"id": "76:2/q19/p3", "position": "The verse invites gratitude for faculties and warns against ingratitude.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says hearing and sight recall favor; Qatāda says the origin story tests recognition of God's rights; Ishlāḥī says awareness of good and evil makes gratitude the test."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q20", "question": "How does this verse relate to nearby verses and other Quranic passages?", "turns_on": "How creation here supplies the argument and narrative progression of the surrounding text.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q20/p1", "position": "It answers 76:1's question of prior nonexistence and leads to 76:3's guidance and outcomes.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the answer to suspense; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the opening question expects assent and denies actual prior human existence, though material existed. Sāmarrāʾī maps the whole sura from origin to afterlife."}, {"id": "76:2/q20/p2", "position": "It parallels creation and resurrection passages, especially Qiyāmah and Muʾminūn.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī links clay in 23:12; Qatāda parallels 23:14. Biqāʿī says the passage counters Qiyāmah's proud deniers (75:3,31–38); Ishlāḥī pairs the suras and contrasts arguments from the reproaching soul (75:2) with creation and recompense. Elmalılı adds 71:14 and 75:14."}, {"id": "76:2/q20/p3", "position": "The sura moves from creation and guidance to reward, punishment and the Prophet's patience.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī outlines this sequence and the closing command to worship."}, {"id": "76:2/q20/p4", "position": "Hearing and sight precede guidance because they convey its evidence and rulings.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says the sensory means normally bring information to the mind before guidance in 76:3."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q21", "question": "How does the verse admit an inward reading?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is read of spiritual components, divine perception or preexistent knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q21/p1", "position": "The mixed human contains contending spiritual powers under divine aid.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān al-Maghribī counts nine: hearing, sight and tongue tempt; self, desire and enemy or Satan oppose faith; intellect, spirit and heart or angel support it. {"id": "76:2/q22", "question": "What concrete creation reports are connected with the verse?", "turns_on": "The different reported durations and persons in creation narratives.", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q22/p1", "position": "The embryo receives the spirit after three forty-day phases.", "reasons": "Bursawī gives drop at forty days, clot at eighty, spirit at 120; Ibn Masʿūd's report has forty days each as drop and clot before an angel writes sex, destiny, provision, effects and lifespan."}, {"id": "76:2/q22/p2", "position": "Adam underwent three forty-year clay phases before the spirit.", "reasons": "A report through al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās lists clay, dark mud and baked or molded clay; Ālūsī also transmits Adam lying between Mecca and Taif for forty years and a tradition that the earlier 'time' has unknown length."}, {"id": "76:2/q22/p3", "position": "Abū Bakr wished creation had ended before testing.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports Rāzī's account as an expression of awareness of unfinished human perfection and future duties."}]}
{"id": "76:2/q23", "question": "What does the verse's divine attribution of testing imply about evil?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:2/q23/p1", "position": "God may attribute an ordeal to Himself, while Quranic phrasing treats evil with care.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says testing Moses' people (20:85) and humanity (67:2; 76:2) is an ordeal, not evil. {"id": "76:3/q01", "question": "Why is divine guidance stated emphatically as 'We guided him'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q01/p1", "position": "The emphatic divine attribution marks guidance as crucial, perhaps even surpassing creation in importance.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says it echoes 'We created' and reasons from creation for worship at 51:56; only the Creator knows the sound way and unaided human reasoning fragments into factions."}]}
{"id": "76:3/q02", "question": "What kind of guidance does 'We guided him' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the guidance is a common disclosure of the way or a disclosure of each person's particular route.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q02/p1", "position": "God makes the way known and its evidence clear; this guidance need not bring the person to the destination.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ defines hidāya as making the way known. Al-Wāḥidī distinguishes showing from creating faith, after which God may enable or abandon; al-Rāzī cites 8:42 and al-Bursawī 90:10. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes showing the route from arrival. Al-Ālūsī says it applies to either response, citing 2:26. Ibn Kathīr prefers the well-known majority account over emergence from the womb."}, {"id": "76:3/q02/p2", "position": "Guidance directs each person along the path of that person's kind, believer toward faith and unbeliever toward disbelief.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya offers this as an alternative while still explaining hadaynāhu as showing, not creating faith."}]}
{"id": "76:3/q03", "question": "By what means does God show the way?", "turns_on": "Whether the note identifies a combined rational and revealed disclosure or singles out innate capacity.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q03/p1", "position": "God uses both human faculties or rational signs and prophetic revelation to make guidance accessible.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī names evidence and messengers; Ibn ʿAṭiyya senses, innate endowment and signs; al-Rāzī senses before intellect, then prophets and books; al-Zamakhsharī rational and transmitted proofs; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī innate prompting and prophetic speech (91:7–8; 30:30); Asad reason, moral instinct and revelation; Study Quran intellect, messengers and signs in revelation, creation and the self (41:53). Al-Biqāʿī adds insight separating divine from human speech; Elmalılı adds origin, destination and duties. Al-Ṭabrisī says accountable people use reason and revelation to attain reward."}, {"id": "76:3/q03/p2", "position": "God endowed people with instinctive awareness of benefit and harm or completed their intellect.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī states the two alternatives; al-Qurṭubī mentions instinct and developed reason; Kur'an Yolu describes capacity to understand one's profit and loss."}]}
{"id": "76:3/q04", "question": "Does this guidance reach every human being in the same way?", "turns_on": "The distinction between universal innate guidance and uneven access to a clear prophetic call.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q04/p1", "position": "Innate guidance belongs universally to human creation, while the spoken religious call reaches societies with unequal individual access.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says distractions and stubbornness weaken innate guidance (45:23); a clear call establishes proof, while those it does not reach clearly are left to divine grace and judgment (4:98). {"id": "76:3/q05", "question": "Why does 'guided him' take 'the path' directly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q05/p1", "position": "Arabic permits the verb with the path directly, or with ilā or li, while conveying that the way is made known.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Wāḥidī explicitly give all three constructions; al-Rāzī repeats them. {"id": "76:3/q06", "question": "What is the path, al-sabīl, that God shows?", "turns_on": "Whether sabīl denotes disclosed moral alternatives, the single true religion, assigned outcomes, innate benefit and harm, or physical birth; Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject the birth reading.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q06/p1", "position": "The paths of good and evil, truth and falsehood, guidance and error are made clear.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī and others name both moral directions; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and Kur'an Yolu cite the two high roads of 90:10. Ibn Kathīr also cites Thamūd at 41:17. Al-Rāzī says the singular is generic and invokes 103:2. Al-Ṭabrisī says evidence allows recognition; al-Bursawī pairs good/evil with salvation/ruin."}, {"id": "76:3/q06/p2", "position": "The path is the true religion, monotheism or Islam, leading to God and felicity.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says proofs and messengers disclose monotheism; al-Ṭabrisī calls it knowledge of religion through reason and revelation; al-Rāzī says only the guidance path deserves the absolute name, whereas an error path is so called relationally (33:67). Ibn Kathīr rejects it for the majority explanation, al-Ālūsī calls it untenable, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it unsound."}, {"id": "76:3/q06/p5", "position": "It is the route of benefit and harm discernible by instinct, or the completion of intellect.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives the alternatives; al-Qurṭubī explains benefits and harms as recognized through instinct and developed reason; Kur'an Yolu speaks of capacity to understand profit and loss."}, {"id": "76:3/q06/p6", "position": "It is each person's own path, the believer's toward faith and the unbeliever's toward disbelief.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives this as an alternative and says 'guided' means showed, not created faith."}]}
{"id": "76:3/q07", "question": "Why portray guidance as showing a path?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q07/p1", "position": "The path depicts God as guide, people as travelers, religious deeds as their road and success as its destination.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this an extended representation; he adds that a traveler may disregard directions and enter danger. {"id": "76:3/q08", "question": "How is immā read in the two alternatives?", "turns_on": "The recorded vowel of the initial hamza and the dialectal or detailed construction attached to the open reading.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q08/p1", "position": "The common reading has kasra and shadda on immā.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls it the common reading and says it functions like 'or'; al-Suyūṭī catalogs its functions with this vocalization, citing 9:106, 18:86, 20:65 and 47:4; Abū Ḥayyān contrasts it with the minority reading."}, {"id": "76:3/q08/p2", "position": "Both instances are read with an open initial vowel, ammā.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites Abū al-ʿAj, identifying him as Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Sulamī, a Syrian governor in Basra. {"id": "76:3/q10", "question": "What do shākiran and kafūran grammatically describe?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of the two accusatives and whether an omitted verb or clause is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q10/p1", "position": "They are circumstantial accusatives of the guided human, describing states or the two groups after guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, Ibn Kathīr, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī attach them to the object pronoun. {"id": "76:3/q11", "question": "What do 'grateful' and 'ungrateful' mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair is glossed by faith, treatment of blessings, ultimate fate, the source of each response, or its recompense.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q11/p1", "position": "They are the believer or monotheist and the unbeliever or polytheist.", "reasons": "Muqātil defines the grateful as one crediting God with creation and the ungrateful as one denying unity or ascribing blessings elsewhere. Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī add fortunate versus wretched."}, {"id": "76:3/q11/p2", "position": "They describe acknowledging or denying God's blessings and acting accordingly.", "reasons": "Qatāda says gratitude or ingratitude toward blessing; Qāshānī says the grateful use faculties in obedience toward the Benefactor while the ungrateful are veiled by gifts and misuse them. {"id": "76:3/q12", "question": "What does the verse imply about human choice and divine action?", "turns_on": "How disclosure of the way relates to divine knowledge and enabling, human willing, and responsibility.", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q12/p1", "position": "God shows the way and people freely choose how to respond, making them accountable.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī says God enables both possibilities and calls through rational and transmitted proofs; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God's will concerns the person's willing, not coercion (80:20; 76:29–30). {"id": "76:3/q13", "question": "Why use the ordinary shākir but intensive kafūr?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:3/q13/p1", "position": "No human can fully thank every divine favor, while ingratitude can be abundant or extreme.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, quoted by al-Qurṭubī, says favors cannot be repaid. ʿAbd al-Jabbār says each thank-you is small beside many gifts but each ingratitude great.
